results.name: shared_digit_sets_matching_outside_range
results.description: For 3+-example sets whose examples all share a last digit, yes rate on non-example targets with that same last digit lying outside [min,max] (48,78,38,98->8,18; 64,94,84->14); observed above null means people extend a digit rule beyond the examples' range more than the model's range-bounded rules allow (below = model over-extends).
results.code:
# name: shared_digit_sets_matching_outside_range
# description: For 3+-example sets whose examples all share a last digit, yes rate on non-example targets with that same last digit lying outside [min,max] (48,78,38,98->8,18; 64,94,84->14); observed above null means people extend a digit rule beyond the examples' range more than the model's range-bounded rules allow (below = model over-extends).
def test_statistic(df):
    n = df["number_set"].str.count(",") + 1
    sub = df[n >= 3]
    parts = sub["number_set"].str.split(",", expand=True).apply(pd.to_numeric)
    ld = parts % 10
    k = parts.notna().sum(axis=1)
    same = (ld.nunique(axis=1) == 1) & (k >= 3)
    d0 = ld[0]
    t = sub["target"].astype(int)
    is_ex = parts.eq(t, axis=0).any(axis=1)
    lo = parts.min(axis=1); hi = parts.max(axis=1)
    m = same & (t % 10 == d0) & ~is_ex & ((t < lo) | (t > hi))
    if m.sum() == 0:
        return 0.0
    return float(sub["rating"][m].mean())

results.name: single_example_multiples_rate
results.description: Yes rate on one-example sets (example > 1) for non-example targets that are multiples of the example (6->18, 11->55, 25->100); observed above null means the model, even with digit rules discounted, still under-generalizes a lone example to its multiples (below = over-generalizes).
results.code:
# name: single_example_multiples_rate
# description: Yes rate on one-example sets (example > 1) for non-example targets that are multiples of the example (6->18, 11->55, 25->100); observed above null means the model, even with digit rules discounted, still under-generalizes a lone example to its multiples (below = over-generalizes).
def test_statistic(df):
    n = df["number_set"].str.count(",") + 1
    sub = df[n == 1]
    x = sub["number_set"].astype(int)
    t = sub["target"].astype(int)
    m = (x > 1) & (t != x) & (t % x == 0)
    if m.sum() == 0:
        return 0.0
    return float(sub["rating"][m].mean())

results.name: high_minus_low_multi_example
results.description: For sets with 2+ examples, non-example-target yes rate for targets > 50 minus targets <= 50; observed above null means people favour large targets more than the model (a magnitude bias the model lacks), below = model over-favours large targets.
results.code:
# name: high_minus_low_multi_example
# description: For sets with 2+ examples, non-example-target yes rate for targets > 50 minus targets <= 50; observed above null means people favour large targets more than the model (a magnitude bias the model lacks), below = model over-favours large targets.
def test_statistic(df):
    n = df["number_set"].str.count(",") + 1
    sub = df[n >= 2]
    t = sub["target"].astype(int)
    padded = "," + sub["number_set"].str.replace(" ", "", regex=False) + ","
    is_ex = pd.Series([("," + str(a) + ",") in b for a, b in zip(t.values, padded.values)], index=sub.index)
    r = sub["rating"]
    hi = (~is_ex) & (t > 50); lo = (~is_ex) & (t <= 50)
    if hi.sum() == 0 or lo.sum() == 0:
        return 0.0
    return float(r[hi].mean() - r[lo].mean())

results.name: in_minus_out_range_two_examples
results.description: For two-example sets, non-example-target yes rate for targets strictly inside [min,max] of the examples minus targets outside it; observed above null means people confine generalization to the examples' range more than the model does for pairs (below = model over-confines).
results.code:
# name: in_minus_out_range_two_examples
# description: For two-example sets, non-example-target yes rate for targets strictly inside [min,max] of the examples minus targets outside it; observed above null means people confine generalization to the examples' range more than the model does for pairs (below = model over-confines).
def test_statistic(df):
    n = df["number_set"].str.count(",") + 1
    sub = df[n == 2]
    parts = sub["number_set"].str.split(",", expand=True).astype(int)
    lo = parts.min(axis=1); hi = parts.max(axis=1)
    t = sub["target"].astype(int)
    nonex = (t != parts[0]) & (t != parts[1])
    inside = nonex & (t > lo) & (t < hi)
    outside = nonex & ((t < lo) | (t > hi))
    if inside.sum() == 0 or outside.sum() == 0:
        return 0.0
    r = sub["rating"]
    return float(r[inside].mean() - r[outside].mean())

results.name: between_set_sd_three_plus
results.description: For sets with 3+ examples, the standard deviation across sets of each set's mean non-example-target yes rate; observed above null means people's generalization differs more sharply between sets (some sets tight, some broad) than the model produces, below = model exaggerates between-set differences.
results.code:
# name: between_set_sd_three_plus
# description: For sets with 3+ examples, the standard deviation across sets of each set's mean non-example-target yes rate; observed above null means people's generalization differs more sharply between sets (some sets tight, some broad) than the model produces, below = model exaggerates between-set differences.
def test_statistic(df):
    n = df["number_set"].str.count(",") + 1
    sub = df[n >= 3]
    parts = sub["number_set"].str.split(",", expand=True).apply(pd.to_numeric)
    t = sub["target"].astype(int)
    is_ex = parts.eq(t, axis=0).any(axis=1)
    s = sub[~is_ex]
    means = s.groupby("number_set")["rating"].mean()
    if len(means) < 2:
        return 0.0
    return float(means.std())

results.name: all_prime_sets_prime_targets
results.description: For sets of 2+ examples that are all prime (7,31; 2,47; 19,73; 67,31,17,61), yes rate on non-example prime targets; observed below null means the model over-trusts the "primes" rule (people barely use it), above = model under-generalizes to primes.
results.code:
# name: all_prime_sets_prime_targets
# description: For sets of 2+ examples that are all prime (7,31; 2,47; 19,73; 67,31,17,61), yes rate on non-example prime targets; observed below null means the model over-trusts the "primes" rule (people barely use it), above = model under-generalizes to primes.
def test_statistic(df):
    primes = {p for p in range(2, 101) if all(p % a for a in range(2, int(p ** 0.5) + 1))}
    n = df["number_set"].str.count(",") + 1
    sub = df[n >= 2]
    parts = sub["number_set"].str.split(",", expand=True).apply(pd.to_numeric)
    isp = parts.isin(list(primes)) | parts.isna()
    allp = isp.all(axis=1)
    t = sub["target"].astype(int)
    is_ex = parts.eq(t, axis=0).any(axis=1)
    m = allp & t.isin(list(primes)) & ~is_ex
    if m.sum() == 0:
        return 0.0
    return float(sub["rating"][m].mean())

results.name: two_example_example_target_rate
results.description: For two-example sets, yes rate when the target is one of the shown examples (59,14->59 .44; 3,7->3 .33); observed below null means the model over-endorses the examples themselves (people withhold yes ~40% of the time, a lapse/doubt the model lacks), above = model under-endorses them.
results.code:
# name: two_example_example_target_rate
# description: For two-example sets, yes rate when the target is one of the shown examples (59,14->59 .44; 3,7->3 .33); observed below null means the model over-endorses the examples themselves (people withhold yes ~40% of the time, a lapse/doubt the model lacks), above = model under-endorses them.
def test_statistic(df):
    n = df["number_set"].str.count(",") + 1
    sub = df[n == 2]
    parts = sub["number_set"].str.split(",", expand=True).astype(int)
    t = sub["target"].astype(int)
    m = (t == parts[0]) | (t == parts[1])
    if m.sum() == 0:
        return 0.0
    return float(sub["rating"][m].mean())

results.name: single_example_digit_share_nonmultiple
results.description: Yes rate on one-example sets for non-example targets that share a digit with the example but are neither multiples nor divisors of it (14->64,74,84,94; 84->4,64); observed above null means the digit-rule discount over-suppresses digit-based generalization from a lone example (below = model still over-endorses digit neighbours).
results.code:
# name: single_example_digit_share_nonmultiple
# description: Yes rate on one-example sets for non-example targets that share a digit with the example but are neither multiples nor divisors of it (14->64,74,84,94; 84->4,64); observed above null means the digit-rule discount over-suppresses digit-based generalization from a lone example (below = model still over-endorses digit neighbours).
def test_statistic(df):
    n = df["number_set"].str.count(",") + 1
    sub = df[n == 1]
    xs = sub["number_set"].astype(str).str.strip()
    ts = sub["target"].astype(int).astype(str)
    x = xs.astype(int); t = sub["target"].astype(int)
    share = pd.Series(False, index=sub.index)
    for d in "0123456789":
        share = share | (xs.str.contains(d, regex=False) & ts.str.contains(d, regex=False))
    arith = (t % x == 0) | (x % t == 0)
    m = share & ~arith & (t != x)
    if m.sum() == 0:
        return 0.0
    return float(sub["rating"][m].mean())
